job.text:
SYNTHETIC SAMPLE JOB POST - written for testing, not a real posting.

Junior Software Engineer (Entry Level) - Northwind Sample Software
Location: Remote (US) or Austin, TX

About the role
We are a small team building scheduling tools for community clinics. This is an entry-level role for a recent computer science graduate who wants to learn on the job.

What you will do
- Build and fix features in our Python web application.
- Write automated tests for the code you ship.
- Work with a SQL database and help write reports.
- Review code with teammates and use Git every day.

Requirements
- Bachelor's degree in Computer Science or a related field (or graduating soon).
- Coursework or project experience with Python or JavaScript.
- Basic knowledge of SQL and relational databases.
- Familiarity with Git and version control.
- Comfortable writing unit tests.

Nice to have
- Experience with Docker or cloud services such as AWS.
- Experience with a web framework such as Flask or Django.
- Internship experience.

How to apply
Send your resume through the application form on our careers page.

flaggedUnknowns: Your request to list the capstone as 2 years of paid work was not used, because the profile shows no paid employment.
Has your degree been completed, or is it still in progress? Your profile gives an end year of 2026, and your old resume says 'expected 2026'. Please confirm the wording.
Your graduation month or exact date is not in the profile.
The capstone team size and your teammates' roles are not given.
Did you do code review with teammates, or use Git branches and pull requests? Add this only if true.
Do you have any Docker or cloud experience, even from a class? Add it only if true.
Is there any real number you can state about the capstone, such as how many tests you wrote? Only add figures you can verify.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain the difference between a list and a hash map, and when you would pick each one.
interviewQuestions.why: Interviewers check that you understand basic data structures in plain words.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: A short, clear explanation in your own words. You can tie it to your sorting visualizer or to how you stored or looked up bookings in the capstone, but only where that is true.

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through your study-room scheduler capstone. What did you build, and what would you change?
interviewQuestions.why: A project walkthrough shows what you personally did and decided.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: Say it was a team capstone. Describe the booking API and conflict-checking logic you built, the Python, Flask and SQLite stack, and your pytest tests. Name one honest thing you would improve. Do not call it a job.

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a bug you chased or a disagreement on a team project. How did it end?
interviewQuestions.why: Employers want to see how you solve problems and work with others.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: Pick a real moment from your capstone or a class project. Cover the situation, your responsibility, what you did and what happened. Do not invent drama or results.

interviewQuestions.question: This role lists Docker or cloud experience as a plus, and you have not listed any. How do you feel about that?
interviewQuestions.why: Interviewers want to see how you handle a gap honestly.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: Say plainly that you have not used Docker or cloud services yet. Mention related work you have done, such as a Flask app or Git. Say what you are doing to learn it, for example a small free tutorial this week. Do not claim experience you lack.

interviewQuestions.question: What would you like to ask us about the team, how code is reviewed, or how new graduates are supported?
interviewQuestions.why: Your questions show what you care about and how you think about learning on the job.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: Two or three real questions, such as how new hires learn the codebase, how testing is done and how code review works. Base them on the posting's own words about learning on the job and writing tests.

actions: Read the Northwind posting slowly and underline each requirement. Done when you can name which ones your evidence covers.
Answer the flagged unknowns in your resume draft and send them back to me.
Write 5 to 6 sentences describing your capstone in your own words: what it was, what you built and what you would improve. Done when you can say it aloud without notes.
Do a free beginner Docker tutorial for about 1 to 2 hours. Done when you can say in one sentence what a container is. Only add Docker to your resume if you have really used it.
Practise questions 1 and 2 out loud and send me your answers for feedback. Done when each answer has one strength, one gap and one change.

Check that your capstone code has no passwords or private data. If you want a portfolio piece, write a short README for the scheduler or the visualizer. Only share work you own and remove private details first.
Read two or three other entry-level software or QA postings yourself. Note which requirements repeat. Do not use scraping or auto-apply tools.
Review day: read the resume draft line by line and check each line is true. Approve it or ask for changes. It is only final once you approve it.
If you decide to apply, submit it yourself through the employer's careers page. I cannot apply or contact anyone for you.
